mediaItem.network: Lava for Good Podcast in association with Signal Company Number One
mediaItem.seriesType: Episodic Series (each episode is generally a standalone story)
mediaItem.focusTheme_Work: Stories of wrongful convictions, exploring contributing factors (like junk science, misconduct), the exoneree's experience, and the path to exoneration through organizations like the Innocence Project.
mediaItem.keyStats:
-   Bite mark analysis has a reported error rate of 91% according to a study mentioned [10:53.200].
-   25 people (including Keith Harward) have been exonerated after being indicted based on bite mark evidence [21:12.000].

featuredIndividual.convictionYear: Trials occurred in 1983 and 1986 [28:24.080]; the conviction leading to the long sentence likely stems from 1986.
featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Circa 2016 (Inferred: Actual perpetrator died in prison in 2006, 10 years before the DNA match definitively identified him [31:46.400])
featuredIndividual.sentence: Capital Murder charge; specific sentence (e.g., life, death) not detailed in transcript [11:07.040].
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness Misidentification (Security guard identification potentially influenced by hypnosis) [11:03.840, 13:00.880, 15:46.640]
Police/Prosecutorial Misconduct (Withholding exculpatory serology report showing perpetrator blood type didn't match Keith's; use of hypnosis on witness) [15:46.640, 27:56.560 - 29:38.000]
innocenceLawyersRaw: Don Salzman, an attorney from the Skadden law firm [03:03.360]. He worked with the Innocence Project, reviewed the case files, highlighted the weakness of the bite mark evidence, pursued DNA testing of the preserved rape kit, and discussed the discovery of withheld exculpatory evidence (the serologist's lab notes).
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: A home invasion occurred near the Newport News shipyard. An intruder broke into a couple's home, beat the husband to death with a crowbar, and then repeatedly sexually assaulted the wife over several hours [05:01.920 - 05:25.680]. The surviving victim stated the attacker wore a sailor's uniform [05:30.960].
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Testimony from multiple forensic odontologists claiming bite marks on the victim's leg matched Keith's dental impressions with high certainty [06:34.400, 10:43.520, 22:57.680 - 23:14.480, 25:11.520 - 26:24.000].

Testimony from a shipyard security guard who identified Keith as a suspicious person he saw entering the shipyard gate around the time of the crime, though this identification came after the guard was hypnotized and his description changed (e.g., adding a mustache that wasn't in the original composite) [11:16.960 - 13:31.840].
Evidence that Keith had bitten his girlfriend during a prior altercation, establishing him as a "biter" [07:43.840 - 08:13.680].
No fingerprint evidence linked Keith to the scene [13:37.360].
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: The transcript does not detail the original trial defense strategy or its effectiveness. However, it notes Keith had a documented alibi: he was attending an alcohol education course in Norfolk (not Newport News) at 6 p.m. on the day before the attack, precisely when the victim reported seeing a suspicious sailor resembling the attacker looking over her fence [14:48.240 - 15:16.800]. It is not stated how or if this alibi was effectively presented at trial. Poor defense representation is mentioned as a common factor in wrongful convictions generally [15:29.200].
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: DNA testing conducted on biological evidence (semen) recovered from the original rape kit (vaginal swabs, victim's thigh, clothing worn after the assault) conclusively excluded Keith Allen-Harward [30:10.560 - 30:22.320].
The same DNA testing identified a positive match to another sailor from the USS Carl Vinson, Jerry Crotty, establishing him as the source of the semen [31:07.680 - 31:24.240, 31:55.840 - 32:25.920].

Discovery of the original forensic serologist's lab notes (previously undisclosed) which indicated the perpetrator's blood type found on swabs was Type O, whereas Keith Harward is Type A. This exculpatory information was not included in the official report or trial testimony [29:14.080 - 29:38.000].
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Jerry Crotty [31:24.240]. He was a fellow sailor serving on the USS Carl Vinson with Keith at the time of the crime [31:14.480]. Crotty was AWOL during part of the initial investigation when dental impressions were being taken [33:35.280]. After leaving the Navy, he committed other crimes, including abduction (kidnapping) and breaking into houses, and was incarcerated in Ohio [31:24.960 - 31:45.760]. He died in prison in Ohio in 2006 [31:46.400]. His DNA was found on multiple items from the crime scene/rape kit [31:55.840 - 32:25.920].

keyQuotesRaw: Keith Harward on mental resilience in prison: "Okay, they already convicted me. They put me in prison, but I wasn't going to allow those criminals. And when I speak of criminals, I'm talking about the police officers and the prosecutors... I wasn't going to let them exact another second for me. They had me, but they weren't going to get my mind." [17:06.960 - 17:27.360]

Don Salzman revealing withheld evidence: "...in his lab notes, it showed that he did get a blood type that was not Keith. It was type O blood, and Keith is type A blood... If that would have been brought up at court... it wouldn't have been a trial." [29:26.880 - 29:43.600]

Keith Harward on the detective's actions: "The detective in my case... after I was convicted, he took one of the molds and went to a foundry and had brass, a brass mold of my teeth made to make a paperweight for his desk. Now, how's that? Knowing what he did. He had to know." [34:04.720 - 34:18.800]

Keith Harward on the importance of innocence organizations: "My heroes, they get up every day... wash their face and brush their teeth and then put the capes on them and they go out saving people. And that's the kind of people that we all should be about." [35:00.560 - 35:09.200]
systemicIssuesRaw: Use and acceptance of Junk Science (specifically bite mark analysis) in court [10:43.520, 23:06.320].
Unreliability of Eyewitness Identification, particularly when influenced by suggestive procedures like hypnosis [11:03.840, 12:16.320].

Police and Prosecutorial Misconduct, including tunnel vision (focusing on a suspect despite contradictory evidence) and Brady violations (failure to disclose exculpatory evidence like the serology notes) [10:22.880, 15:46.640, 27:56.560].
Pressure on law enforcement to solve high-profile, violent crimes, potentially leading to rushed judgments and errors [06:12.320].
Lack of regulation and scientific validation for certain forensic disciplines presented as expert testimony [23:23.760].
The difficulty exonerees face in prison, often unaware of organizations that could help [20:28.160].
policyRecommendationsRaw: Strong encouragement to support and donate to the Innocence Project [35:18.400, 35:27.840].
Need to raise public awareness about the existence and work of innocence organizations [34:32.160].
Implicit call to abandon the use of bite mark evidence in criminal courts.
Implicit call for stricter protocols around eyewitness identification and the prohibition of techniques like hypnosis to "enhance" memory for testimony.
Implicit call for accountability for prosecutorial misconduct, particularly the withholding of exculpatory evidence.
personalNarrativeRaw: Keith describes the jarring transition from a normal life to being arrested and imprisoned ("Roach Motel" [02:25.200]). He maintained his belief in his innocence throughout his 33 years of incarceration, which fueled his mental survival [16:27.600]. He adopted a mindset of refusing to let the officials who wronged him ("the criminals") break his spirit or take more from him than his physical freedom [17:06.960 - 17:41.920]. Keith expresses significant empathy for the original victim, highlighting how the failure to catch the real perpetrator and his own wrongful conviction re-victimized her decades later when the truth emerged [32:25.920 - 33:14.160]. He holds innocence advocates in high regard, calling them "heroes" [35:00.560].
